jw_1969_montreal_01.text: 1969: Departure for Québec. Based on a novel by Réjean Ducharme, L'Avalée des avalés. Exhibited at the French Pavilion in Montréal; the photo is of poor quality.

jw_1970_montreal_02.title: Aluchromies and various exhibitions
jw_1970_montreal_02.text: At the request of the Alcan plants, Jeannette experimented with oxidized aluminum and pigments derived from wool dyeing: thus her aluchromies were born. Exhibitions: Galerie Art Pictural, 1971; S.A.P.Q, Place Bonaventure, Montréal, 1972; Université de Montréal, January 1973; Salon de l'aluminium de Chicoutimi, May 1973; Université de Sherbrooke, May 1973.

jw_1978_lyon_03.title: Two north windows of the Chapel of Saint Joseph
jw_1978_lyon_03.text: Back from Québec, 1974: a work order was issued for the Chapel of Saint Joseph. Canon Manien chose the theme of the genealogy of Christ and followed its iconography; the execution, carried out “with a comb” in the family workshop, was completed quickly.

jw_1978_paris_04.title: Stained-glass window for a laboratory
jw_1978_paris_04.text: Stained-glass window for my husband, Bernard Weiss, in his laboratory on rue Manin. Now in a private collection.

jw_1980_paris_06.title: Figure emerging from the glass
jw_1980_paris_06.text: Published in the 1st Salon du Vitrail of the Centre International du Vitrail (1980) and in Métiers d'Art (1982) by Françoise Perrot.

jw_1981_beauvais_01.title: The Life of Tobias
jw_1981_beauvais_01.text: The Life of Tobias, along with two abstract infills (next page) made for the Église Saint-Étienne de Beauvais, enters into dialogue with the windows of the Le Prince family, 16th-century glassmakers from Beauvais. My intention was to rebalance the composition of lancets taken from different windows while keeping my own personal graphic style. I worked with grisaille and silver stain to reconcile the figurative elements inherited from the 16th century with contemporary figurative idioms — sometimes abstract — and to blend them into a single harmony, preserving the soft light characteristic of the Le Prince windows. Referenced in an article by Chantal Bouchon.

jw_1983_beauvais_03.title: Two infills
jw_1983_beauvais_03.text: The first infill is a window dedicated to Saint Nicholas, containing at the top of the left lancet a very fine ship by Jean Le Prince. The two right-hand lancets hold panels that came from another window.

1983_beauvais_fontaine_01.jpg.alt: In the second infill, in the left lancet, on panels executed by Engrand Le Prince, a tall figure points to the soul rising from the dead man being carried to his tomb. The panels of the next two lancets show the Fountain of Life attributed to the Master of Montmorency, which should have been laid out across all three lancets. Jean Taralon, Inspector General of Historic Monuments, had told me that after the surviving elements from different windows were reinstalled in these two bays, he, my father and Louis Grodecki had marveled at these panels, whose beauty had been brought back to light. I obtained scaffolding beneath the windows so that I could execute the accompanying cartoons for the work, which was meant to showcase and rebalance the mismatched old panels. Up on that scaffolding I felt an incredible happiness, among the Le Princes and the Master of Montmorency. The photos show the windows before and after the infills.

jw_1984_darmannes_02.title: Two stained-glass windows in the transept
jw_1984_darmannes_02.text: For the Romanesque transept, whose 19th-century ironwork was kept, I made the light play with brown and black grisailles on clear glass. Jean Taralon regarded this work as an exemplary creation for its integration into Romanesque architecture (Métier d'Art, no. 32, October 1986).

jw_1985_beauvais_04.title: A window in the south transept chapel
jw_1985_beauvais_04.location_in_building: Chapel of Saint Vincent de Paul
jw_1985_beauvais_04.text: Creation of 20 m² of accompanying glass to showcase a 15th-century Picard donor and, on the left, a later figure. In homage to the 15th century, I used, as in their sumptuous glazing, many expanses of glass painted in grisaille.

jw_1986_champagne_01.title: Twelve stained-glass windows in the nave
jw_1986_champagne_01.text: Twelve stained-glass windows in the nave, one window in the portal of the south nave, two windows in the north and south transept arms, and a small façade rose window.

jw_1988_pontstemaxence_02.title: Two windows in the south nave
jw_1988_pontstemaxence_02.text: In this very dark nave, I proposed very light windows on maquettes, and I executed them mostly in clear glass painted with grisaille, accompanied by a few touches of silver stain and small pieces of green glass. It is one of my favorite works, because it was a true work of light, the building being very dark.

jw_1991_niort_01.title: Tree of Jesse - Infills and restoration
jw_1991_niort_01.text: My proposal for showcasing the Tree of Jesse won the competition. Some of the kings date from the 15th century; the other old panels are from the 17th and 19th centuries. My infills are abstract, except for 4 kings, whose crowns I replaced with hats. Because of the tie bars running through the mullions, I had to place the large 17th-century prophet in a register at the base, the only register in which the panel could fit in its entirety. Nathalie Frachon-Gielarek, who was in charge of the restoration, followed my work in a spirit of friendship. To my great joy, two kings were rediscovered, which I was able to set higher up in place of mine, and the large prophet in place of one of my abstract panels.

jw_1991_amiens_01.title: Creation and restoration with infills
jw_1991_amiens_01.location_in_building: Chapel of Saint Francis of Assisi
jw_1991_amiens_01.text: I was entrusted with the rearrangement of the 13th-century stained glass from the cathedral choir. The windows, removed during the First World War, had been ravaged by a fire that broke out in a cabinetmaker's workshop: the remaining panels were incomplete, with molten lead on charred and shattered glass. The main photo shows the final state. With the approval of Historic Monuments, I chose not to make my creations and infills in the central window too dark, unlike the eighteen charred borders and the 13th-century elements of the five medallions. My creations are simply a little less light than those of the two windows on either side of it. My work was overseen by Nathalie Frachon-Gielarek, stained-glass historian and research officer.

jw_1994_martyre_01.title: Infills for the 16th-century Breton Tree of Jesse
jw_1994_martyre_01.text: Having won the competition with abstract maquettes, I proposed to Historic Monuments that I adapt to the wishes of the master, the rector and the parishioners by designing, in alternation, allusive or figurative windows relating to an iconography. I spent a month in La Martyre completing in situ the full-size colored cartoon of the 16th-century Tree of Jesse, in order to immerse myself in the atmosphere inside the church and to harmonize my infills with the magnificent Dormition, a 16th-century Breton stained-glass window located in a choir chapel next to the Tree of Jesse.

jw_1994_martyre_02.title: Five windows in harmony with the Tree of Jesse
jw_1994_martyre_02.text: For all the windows, the palette and the main color accents of the abstract maquettes were retained. The project, carried out with excellent momentum, was praised. A later defect, however, browned the windows: the grisaille used, although certified, turned out to be non-compliant. Laboratory investigations are underway. Here, the main photo shows, from left to right, Jacob's Ladder, the Manna in the Desert during the Exodus, and the Tree of Jesse presented earlier.

jw_2001_saverne_01.title: Eighteen stained-glass windows in the north and south naves
jw_2001_saverne_01.text: The embankment, with its trees, and the mountain barely let any light into the north nave. The coloring of the cartoons corresponds to the colors chosen for the execution of these windows. After the cartoons had been made to the dimensions of the windows, the masons narrowed all the openings. All the cartoons had to be redone to the new dimensions. This work suffered the same damage as La Martyre.
